4288.heavy: Not stated. The author calls the predictable placement 'quantity-sensitive' (pp. 51, 409) but gives no heavy-syllable criterion anywhere in the grammar (a full-text search for quantity/weight/heavy/mora finds only these two sentences); the examples show that a closed (CVC) final syllable does not attract the accent (éyrir, éfej, éfer, áhin, óduy, ótuy, ómuy, ónuy, edíder, egédid, ednórur; p. 52), and the language has no vowel length or phonemic vowel sequences within syllables (§2.2.3 p. 47). 'Quantity-sensitive' appears to be used loosely as a synonym of 'predictable'.
4288.prule: Culminative pitch accent: one high-toned accented syllable per polysyllabic word, other syllables low/neutral. Where placement is predictable (the general case for roots), the accent falls on the penultimate syllable of the root: exx. 116-121 óko, éra, yú.a, déci, éyrir, éfej, óduy, edíder, mahína, oysúra, ofóga; monosyllabic roots accented (már, ég, ní). Table 2 p. 410: eféga, cíyja, ébah, móga, órna, mogósa, meybága, meméga.
4288.srule: None in simplex words: 'only one fixed accent per polysyllabic word' (p. 51), other syllables low or neutral (p. 49); no rhythmic or alternating accent is described; prefixes, circumfix, enclitic -o and paragogic -a are unaccented and mos- compounds keep a single accent on the noun root (p. 102), as do lexicalized compounds (p. 105); ordinary noun compounds are said to carry an accent on both roots (§3.1.4 p. 99). Additional accent also in reduplicated forms: the reduplicant takes an accent when the copied root segment is accented (áht-áhta, ósk-óska, egés-gés(a), tók-tók(a), orówi-ówi, p. 55), not ranked as primary vs secondary by the source.

4288.tone: The source classifies Moskona explicitly as a pitch-accent language (§1.3.2 p. 8 'the prosodic system is pitch accent'; §2.3 p. 49; Appendix A p. 409 'pitch accent languages with only one tone melody'), of the culminative type: a single tonal contrast, high tone on the one accented syllable per word, other syllables low or neutral, 'the accent functioning like the main stress in a stress system'. Contrasted with the lexical-tone languages Abun and Mpur and the stress languages Hatam (metrical stress) and Maybrat (lexical stress) in the same area (p. 49). Acoustic correlates (§2.3.1 pp. 50-51): pitch change is the main component, with greater amplitude and usually greater duration, but the pitch difference can be as small as 0.6 semitones with amplitude the stronger cue, and duration 'does not always correlate with accent'. Accented syllables are written with an acute accent; in chapters after ch. 2 only roots with unpredictable accent are marked (p. 49).

4289.prule: No word stress/accent: in an instrumental study (F0, duration, pauses) of read and spontaneous speech of the Ouagadougou standard dialect, no accentuation could be detected, so no prosodic word can be defined on stressed syllables. Mooré is a two-tone (H, L) terraced-level tone language with downdrift and downstep; the syllable is the tone-bearing unit; prosodic grouping is carried by intonation (F0 declination and reset, pauses, final lengthening at unit boundaries), not by stressed syllables.

tn.quote: Le mooré est une langue à ton ponctuel. ... L’unité porteuse de ton en mooré est la syllabe. ... Cependant, Peterson (1971) et Kinda (1984) distinguent deux tons pertinents en mooré, mais qui sont réalisés en trois tons. ... Il y a en fait un phénomène de surface, l’abaissement tonal (downstep), qui se produit en mooré. C’est ce phénomène qui est perçu comme le troisième ton réalisé dans la structure de surface. ... Ainsi le mooré ne possède que deux tons qui ont trois niveaux de réalisation. Platiel et Kaboré (1998) déterminent eux aussi deux tons ponctuels en mooré.
tn.translation: Mooré is a level-tone (register-tone) language. ... The tone-bearing unit in Mooré is the syllable. ... However, Peterson (1971) and Kinda (1984) distinguish two relevant tones in Mooré, which are realised as three tones. ... There is in fact a surface phenomenon, tonal lowering (downstep), which occurs in Mooré. It is this phenomenon that is perceived as the third tone realised in the surface structure. ... Thus Mooré has only two tones, which have three levels of realisation. Platiel and Kaboré (1998) likewise establish two level tones in Mooré.

4293.prule: SUBGROUP-INFERRED (no opened text pairs the names Mpalityan or Lutiɣ with a stress statement). Group-level statement covering Mpalityan and Lutiɣ (listed p. 163 among the 13 Northern Paman samples): primary stress, 'a strictly phonetic feature' (non-contrastive), shifted from the initial to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem (*CV2) in all Northern Paman languages, after which *C1 was lost invariably and short *V1 lost, retained or metathesized (for Mpalityan and Lutiɣ, p. 173 of the same paper: 'sometimes lost, sometimes retained, and sometimes metathesized'). Synchronically the stressed syllable is the first vowel preceded by a consonant: word-initial in consonant-initial words, second syllable in vowel-initial words. Hale states that synchronic form only for Linngithigh (p. 179) and, in Hale 1976b (excerpt only), for Uradhi as 'apparently shared by all of the Northern Paman languages'. Position is conditioned on whether the word begins in a vowel (a segmental condition), not on syllable count or weight. Because in Mpalityan and Lutiɣ short *V1 'was sometimes lost, sometimes retained, and sometimes metathesized' (p. 173), both consonant-initial and vowel-initial words are expected, so the onset condition (initial stress vs second-vowel stress) bites in this language more often than in the languages south of it, where short *V1 'was ordinarily lost' (p. 173).

Ce tonème se réalise phonétiquement par une descente rapide de la voix d'un ton haut à un ton bas. 1.1.4 TONEME MONTANT ... Ce tonème se réalise phonétiquement "bas relevé". ... [p. 50] Le système tonal du mpumpuŋ est fait de quatre tonèmes: haut, bas, montant, descendant. ... [p. 56] En Mpumpuŋ, l'unique voie de définition de la syllabe, c'est la présence d'un tonème dont le support est une voyelle.
tn.translation: Mpumpuŋ is a tone language. ... tone has a distinctive function in it. Our investigations yield the following four tonemes: ... 1.1.3 FALLING TONEME ... This toneme is realised phonetically by a rapid drop of the voice from a high tone to a low tone. 1.1.4 RISING TONEME ... This toneme is realised phonetically as 'raised low'. ... [p. 50] The tonal system of Mpumpuŋ consists of four tonemes: high, low, rising, falling. ... [p. 56] In Mpumpuŋ, the only way of defining the syllable is the presence of a toneme whose support is a vowel.

4296.tone: Odé 2002 §2 (p. 48): 'Mpur is a language with lexical tone contrasts. To my knowledge it is, together with the neighbouring Abun language (Berry & Berry 1999), the only Non-Austronesian tone language in the Bird's Head area.' §2.3 (p. 50): 'three tones have been attested in Mpur: high, mid and low. The issue still is whether a fourth midrising tone, existing on the perceptual level, is phonologically significant.' Levels: H 12 ST, M 7 ST, L 0 (Table 3, p. 51); tone sandhi normal, no downdrift/downstep, some declination. Odé 1997 p. 183: 'a classification into five perceptual lexical tone contrasts has been arrived at: four level tones (high, mid, midlow and low) and one contour tone (falling&rising)...; there are some dialectal differences. There is no evidence for phonemic lexical stress in Mpur.' On stress/accent: no phonologically significant lexical stress; word 'accent' in the utterance is expressed by focus marker ni, enclitics or repetition (§2.5).

4297.tone: Stilson 1866 neither marks nor mentions tone. The modern primary phonology, Hornéy 2012 (A phonological analysis of Mro Khimi, UND MA thesis) states 'Mro Khimi has two contrastive tones, H and L, which form four tone melodies... Affixes are underlyingly toneless', falling tones only phrase-finally; the strings 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' do not occur in Hornéy's text (a full-text search confirmed), only 'The minor syllable does have a surface vowel, which has a much shorter duration than vowels in other syllables'. So the language is tonal with root-final (major-syllable) prominence; the only explicit placement statement is Stilson's 1866 impressionistic 'accent'. A verifier who reads the 1866 'accent' as non-stress (tone/length percept) would reclassify it as tone or pitch accent; I keep fixed and quantity-insensitive because the house code for tone languages applies only where no stress rule is stated, and one is stated here.

tn.quote: Mro Khimi has two contrastive tones, H and L. Like Mara, there are no rising tones, and falling tones only occur phrase-finally. Mro Khimi has four tone melodies on the roots, L H LH and HL, toneless affixes, tone on suffixes spreading from roots, and polar tone on prefixes. ... Nasalized vowels and oral vowels are the only Tone Bearing Units (TBUs) in Mro Khimi. ... Since Mro Khimi does not permit contour tones, the final tones in words with more tones than syllables, such as the final L in /kʰøHL/ ‘country’, are left floating, resulting in [kʰǿ].

4298.tone: Three basic tones, each with a freely fading (open) variant and a glottal-stop-bounded variant; the 'Tonakzent' is the tone itself, a fixed property of the syllable with no detachable function, subject only to slurring in connected speech. Syllables closed by k, t, p also carry one of the three tones but without the variant contrast; some verbs add an implosive -k as a third, syntactically conditioned variant, and the tone of a stop-closed syllable equals that of the open syllable. Tones I/II/III correspond historically to the Burmese level, heavy and creaky (Kurzton) tones; Arakanese loans ending in a hard glottal stop take final -k and tone IIa (p. 521). The source says nothing about a stressed syllable in polysyllabic Mru words; its 'Hauptton'/'Betonung' remarks (p. 507) concern the ethnonym Khumi/Khami/kimmi in old vocabularies, not Mru.

4304.dq: The data show that there are three different word tone systems in the Tibetan languages studied here: tone template, word tone, and syllable tone. In the tone template languages (Dolpo and Mugom Tibetan), the four monosyllabic patterns are reduced to two disyllabic pitch patterns, and these patterns are derived from the register of the first syllable.

4304.prule: Word tone of the 'tone template' type: the contrastive pitch (high vs. low register; the monosyllable's level/falling contrast is neutralized, four patterns reducing to two) is carried by the first syllable of the word only; non-initial syllables take the fixed pitch of the template regardless of their citation-form pitch. The source states no word-stress rule for Mugom.
4304.srule: Not mentioned in Watters 2002 (secs. 6-8, pp. 32-48 read): the article states no word stress of any kind, primary or secondary, for Mugom; it analyses Mugom as a first-syllable 'tone template' word-tone language, and its only 'stress' remarks concern Lhasa (p. 33), Dolpo (pp. 34-35, a transcription clue) and Lhomi (pp. 40, 43).

4304.tone: p. 32: 'The acoustic data studied for this paper point to three kinds of tone systems within the general Himalayan tone typology: syllable based tone, as in Lhomi and Dzongkha; word tone templates, as in Dolpo and Mugom Tibetan; and word tone where one particular tone pattern extends over the whole word, as in Sherpa.' p. 48 (scan): 'Dolpo and Mugom Tibetan where the four monosyllabic patterns are reduced to two pitch patterns, derived from the register of the first syllable'. Every occurrence of 'stress'/'unstressed' in the article (scan a full-text search, 11 hits) belongs to the Lhasa template summary (p. 33), the Dolpo data of sec. 6.1.2 (p. 34 'the second syllable is unstressed' for Dolpo 'dust'; p. 35 'a helpful auditory clue is listening for a perceived stress on the second syllable (high register)', a transcriber's heuristic), the Lhomi sections (pp. 40, 43) and the introduction's quotation of Sprigg 1966 (p. 2). None is tied to Mugom data, so no stress statement exists for Mugom; the language is coded as a word-tone system with no stress rule.

variants.prule: Primary stress always on the final syllable of the word (quantity-insensitive; diphthongs and triphthongs count as one final-syllable nucleus, stressed on their first element).
variants.quote: [p. 62-63] Synchronically, Merap and Murik could not be more different. Merap has strong word-final stress, 26 vowels including diphthongs, triphthongs, length, and nasality distinctions, while Murik is a conservative language, even by Kayanic standards, and has weak penultimate stress with a standard six vowel inventory of i, e, a, o, u, and ə. [p. 68] Justifying the above vowel inventory is dependent on one’s analysis of stress. Merap is a stress-final language, where the final syllable is always stressed. In every vowel phoneme presented above, stress falls on the initial segment. Thus, a is stressed as [ˈa], əw is stressed [ˈəw], ĩə̯ is stressed [ˈĩə̯], and ayə̯ is stressed [ˈayə̯]. If, for example, one were to interpret ayə̯ as ayə, that is, with the schwa as a separate syllable, one would have to explain why stress is penultimate [ˈa.yə] and not final [a.ˈyə]. Some words do have legitimate vowel clusters, like kiawə̯ ‘the Myna bird’ which is stressed [kiˈawə̯] and reflects *kiuŋ. [p. 72] ... words with CVCCVC structures receive a secondary stress in Merap; ˌCVCˈCVC.

4311.dq: If most occurrences of word-final accent are attributed to sentence intonation, what remains should be mostly word stress. (p. 97) ... That the second-syllable stress is a feature of the word, and not (exclusively) sentence intonation, is shown by occurrences of /hara/ in other parts of the sentence (p. 99)
4311.dloc: Ch. 1 Phonology, sec. 140 'Stress and Intonation' (p. 95), sec. 141 'Intonation vs. Stress' (p. 96), sec. 142 'Stress Assignment' (pp. 97-103); domain passages diss. p. 97 and p. 99.
4311.heavy: Okrand never uses the terms heavy/light. The conditioning he states is syllable shape plus vowel length: a disyllable with an open initial syllable and an (underlying) long vowel in its second syllable — surface /CVCV(C)/ after final-vowel shortening — is stressed on that second syllable; a disyllable whose initial syllable is closed (rúkka, húttuy) or has a long vowel (ká:lis, lá:pis) is stressed initially; in words of three or more syllables stress is initial regardless of vowel length (kámi:sa, kórotka). So, in effect, a CVC or CV: initial syllable holds the stress, a bare CV initial syllable in a disyllable cedes it to the final syllable.
4311.dflt: Initial syllable in words of three or more syllables (Okrand's 'normal stress assignment rule'); in a disyllable with a bare CV initial syllable (/CVCV(C)/, no closed or long initial syllable) the second, final syllable.
4311.prule: Stress is non-phonemic (predictable). Default: first syllable of the word. Exception class defined by syllable shape and vowel length: disyllabic words of surface shape /CVCV(C)/ (open, short initial syllable; underlying ||CVCV:(C)|| whose long final vowel is shortened) are stressed on the second syllable (koró 'foot', hará 'gives', tawáh 'work', waráy 'cut it!'). Disyllables with a closed or long initial syllable (rúkka, húttuy, ká:lis, lá:pis) and all words of three or more syllables, whatever their vowel lengths, take initial stress (kámi:sa, kámpana, mánteka, póyi:tu, kórotka, níya:tum); with a few exceptions, Spanish loans take initial stress regardless of Spanish stress.
4311.srule: Exists, placement not given: Okrand reads Harrington's grave accent and circled acute accent, which (almost) never occur alone, as 'secondary stress' or a syllable of lesser prominence, but gives no rule for where they fall; his stress-assignment rules place one stress per word.

4312.tone: Register tone: H, B (low), M (mid, only on CV stems); rising and falling contours rare 'au niveau du lexique'. Tone is lexically distinctive (the thesis's Mwesa forms are tone-marked, e.g. dìbɛ́yɛ̀ 'sein', ànùmbà 'odeur', mbázá 'jumeau'; Part II §II.1.2 tabulates Mwesa tonal reflexes of *HB/*HH/*BB/*BH stems). No stress or accent statement for Mwesa anywhere in the 382-page thesis (a full-text search for accent/accentu/stress/proémin/intensité/tonique: 3 hits, none about Mwesa). The only accent-related passage is a B20 group-level diachronic speculation at p. 238, closing paragraph of §II.1.2 'Analyses supra segmentales', verified verbatim: 'La quasi-absence d'opposition tonale H/B amorcée en T2, vient du fait que la syllabe finale des thèmes est régulièrement réalisée avec un ton bas. Tels qu'observés, les faits pourraient conforter comme l'ont suggéré, J, P. Rekanga (2007. p. 26) et E. Dodo-Bouguendza (2010. p. 78) une évolution vers un processus accentuel.' Mwesa is named on that page only as one of four parlers (with kota, màhɔ̀ŋgwɛ́, ndambomo) not attesting *BB > HB. This is a diachronic tendency claim about the group, not a synchronic stress rule for Mwesa.

tn.quote: Le système tonal du mwesa contient trois registres de base: le tonème haut (H), le tonème bas (B) et le tonème moyen (M). Ce dernier tonème est plutôt rare, et on ne le rencontre que sur des thèmes CV. On trouve par ailleurs deux tons modulés en mwesa: le ton montant et le ton descendant. Les tons modulés sont cependant assez rares comparés aux tons ponctuels, du moins au niveau du lexique. ... Nous avons considéré que les tons complexes du mwesa résultent de la combinaison de deux tons ponctuels (BH et HB), comme dans yôm (‘mari’), qui alterne avec yómì ~ yómò.
tn.translation: The Mwesa tone system contains three basic registers: the high toneme (H), the low toneme (B) and the mid toneme (M). The latter toneme is rather rare and is found only on CV stems. There are also two modulated tones in Mwesa: the rising tone and the falling tone. The modulated tones are however fairly rare compared with the level tones, at least in the lexicon. ... We have taken the complex tones of Mwesa to result from the combination of two level tones (BH and HB), as in yôm ('husband'), which alternates with yómì ~ yómò.

tn.quote: Naba is a tonal language, with three level tones, High (H), Mid (M) and Low (L). The majority of words, especially nouns and verbs, have an underlying tone melody which consists either of one level tone or a sequence of levels. However, a good number of grammatical function morphemes, such as clitics, particles, and verbal affixes, are underlyingly toneless. ... From the examples in the right column it is shown that in Naba tone attaches to moras rather than to syllables. VV sequences that form a single syllable can carry two different tones.
tn.cite: Scherrer, Elaine Marie. 2022. A phonological description of Naba. Afrika und Übersee 95: 76-134. Hamburg University Press. DOI 10.15460/auue.2022.95.1.255.
tn.locator: p. 95, section 4 'Tone' (opening paragraph) and section 4.1 'Tone-bearing units'
tn.note: Three level tones H, M, L; the mora is the TBU (VV syllables carry two tones). Words take one of nine lexical melodies; some clitics and affixes toneless, M default. Automatic downstep only. Checked against the source (tone consistency check round 3, 2026-09-24): downstep no -> yes (pp. 103-104, section 4.4.2 'Downstep').

corr.words: 4.4.2 Downstep A L tone at the end of one morpheme may downstep a H or M tone at the beginning of the following morpheme. This automatic downstep does not create a complete lowering; H is not downstepped to M nor is M downstepped to L, but a slight lowering can be perceived. ... This type of automatic downstep occurs throughout the language ... Non-automatic downstep, caused by floating L tone, is not attested in Naba

4314.tone: Source states: 'Nabit is also a tonal language with two tones, a high tone and a low tone. Tone is rarely contrastive though meaning that if a word is said with the incorrect tone it does not usually affect the meaning.' (p. 80, p. 90), and earlier: 'Based on my analysis I discovered that although high and low tones exist in Nabit, these tones do not affect native speaker's ability to understand a word or phrase, but several speakers pointed out that when I said words with the incorrect tone they sounded wrong.' (p. 44, p. 54; the sentence opens at the foot of p. 43 / top of p. 44); the orthography marks tone only where meaning is ambiguous. The only stress vocabulary in the whole text is incidental: 'the tendency to drop unstressed vowels', e.g. 'fire' 'usually pronounced [bugəm] with an unstressed second vowel' (p. 93, p. 103; also [sɛg̃ər] 'forest' spelled <sɛg̃r>); a full-text search of the full text for 'stress'/'accent'/'prominen'/'pitch'/'intonation' yields no other phonological use (remaining hits: 'financial stress', 'stress the importance', 'seamstress', 'accentuate(d)', 'prominent' themes/ideologies). The p. 10 Dakubu e-mail ('Talene, Nabit, and Kusaal all tend to weaken and drop the final vowel in a trisyllabic word, CVCVCV, whereas Gurenɛ usually weakens the second vowel') is a vowel-reduction remark, not a stress rule. Nothing licenses a fixed-initial reading; the reduction of non-initial vowels is at most consistent with it.
